newsitem.title: USA: Hewlett-Packard takes on Silicon Graphics.
newsitem.headline: Hewlett-Packard takes on Silicon Graphics.

text.p: Hewlett-Packard Co. said Tuesday it will introduce a speedy new three-dimensional graphics computer system that challenges Silicon Graphics Inc.'s grip on high-end graphics supercomputing.

Analysts said the system, which Hewlett-Packard dubbed the HP Visualize PxFl, will be between 40 and 100 times faster than the best systems currently available. It is due to be be shipped in the first quarter of 1998.

John Austin, manager of research and development at Hewlett-Packard's Chapel Hill, N.C., graphics laboratory, said the new system aims to take on Silicon Graphics' dominant position in the billion-dollar market for graphics supercomputing.
"This is a revolutionary new architecture," Austin said of the new system.

Joel Orr, president of Orr Associates International in Chesapeake, Va., said the system would help Hewlett-Packard consolidate its No. 2 position in the market and challenge Silicon Graphics (SGI) directly.

"HP has always been a fascinating second runner," he said. "They've always been less sexy than SGI and from time to time they've even had performance that exceeded SGI, but when they did they never knew how to take advantage of that."
The new technology, developed at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and licensed by Hewlett-Packard, will aid mechanical engineers such as designers of aircraft and automobiles.

"This HP advance is a quantum leap," said Orr. "Tenfold increases of speed are perceived of as qualitative improvements, so having stuff being 40 to 100 times as fast as what went before is really different.
"That means things that took a day now take minutes. I think this will definitely be a wakeup call to SGI," he added.
Silicon Graphics officials were not immediately available to comment.

HP said the new technology, which had been code-named Everest because, according to techical computing director Jim Christiansen, "it was the highest peak in the world" for computer performance, will be available in systems which will be priced from just above $100,000 to more than $1 million.
The products can be ordered beginning next week when the new line is formally launched.

The introduction is the second of a three-step, 120-day campaign for the graphics market by Hewlett-Packard, which earlier this year unveiled plans to use a new technology to bring graphics capability to desktops.
Later this year, the company plans to introduce high-end graphics boards which are expected to greatly accelerate the speed of graphics on workstations and personal computers.
